141.title: Small groups
141.hook: Wesley's class meetings asked one question: how is it with your soul?
141.carry: how is it with your soul?
141.howItsDone: Many Christians belong to a small group that meets weekly in a home or at church to read the Bible, pray and talk honestly about their lives; Methodist class meetings and their question 'how is it with your soul?' are one historic model.

segments.voice: Yesterday, koinonia, sharing a common life, the first believers eating together from house to house. Your line: you weren't meant to do it alone. Today, how small that sharing can get.
screen: `YOU WEREN'T MEANT TO DO IT ALONE.`

segments.voice: How are you? Fine. You? Good, busy. It's so quick it barely counts as a question. Now step into a room of about a dozen people, farmers, miners, maids, shopkeepers, in eighteenth-century England, meeting on a weeknight. A leader goes around the circle and asks each person the same question. Not how are you. Not how's work. How is it with your soul? And each person has to answer. Honestly. In front of the others. Every single week.
screen: `FINE. YOU? GOOD, BUSY.` → `A DOZEN PEOPLE, ONE QUESTION.` → `HOW IS IT WITH YOUR SOUL?`

segments.voice: Bristol, England, 1742. The Methodists, the movement led by John Wesley, owe money on their new meeting house. Someone suggests a practical fix: divide the members into groups of about twelve, and have a leader collect a penny a week from each. But the leaders, going door to door for their pennies, keep finding things out: a man drinking again, a family that can't eat. Wesley saw what was happening and made it the heart of the movement. The class meeting was born. Once a week, each class met with its leader. They sang, they prayed, and the leader asked each one about their life with God. The question tradition remembers them by is today's line: how is it with your soul? The classes could do something a sermon couldn't. You can hide in a crowd of a thousand. You can't hide in a circle of twelve people who know your name. Jesus had said something that makes small numbers matter. In the King James Bible: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Two or three is enough. The idea has spread far beyond Methodism: home groups, cell groups, Bible studies around kitchen tables, Catholic small faith communities. All of them share the same bet: people change less from being taught at and more from being known. Wesley's version started with pennies.
screen: `BRISTOL, 1742: A PENNY A WEEK.` · `THE LEADERS KEEP FINDING THINGS.` · `YOU CAN'T HIDE IN A CIRCLE OF TWELVE.` · `CHANGED BY BEING KNOWN.` · then, large: `WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED.`

segments.voice: Ask the question of yourself first: how is it with your soul, not your calendar or your inbox, your soul, whatever that word means to you right now. Let the honest answer come, even if it's tired, or muddled, or better than you expected. Then think of one person you could really ask, someone who'd get past fine if they knew you meant it, and if you pray, pray for them by name.
Small groups. A dozen people, meeting weekly, known by name. Wesley's class meetings turned a penny collection into honest care.
Your line: how is it with your soul? Fine is allowed, but it isn't the whole answer. Until next time.

142.title: Bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2)
142.hook: carrying each other's loads is how the law of Christ is kept
142.howItsDone: Many churches organize meals, visits, rides and prayer for members going through illness, grief or hardship, and many Christians take Galatians 6:2 as a description of what church should be.

segments.voice: Yesterday, small groups, and your line: how is it with your soul? Today, when the answer is heavy.

Moving day. You've boxed up your whole life, and the couch is at the bottom of three flights of stairs. Alone, it's impossible; you'd wreck your back and the wall. Then two friends show up, one on each end, and suddenly it's awkward, funny and done in ten minutes. The same weight, split, becomes something else. Paul, writing to the churches in Galatia, reaches for that picture. He's argued for five chapters about rules and freedom, and near the end he gives an instruction that sounds a lot like moving day.
screen: `THREE FLIGHTS, ONE COUCH.` → `TWO FRIENDS SHOW UP.` → `THE SAME WEIGHT, SPLIT.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." The Galatians have been arguing about which laws Christians must keep. And Paul says: you want a law? Here's the law of Christ. Carry each other. Not a new rulebook. Love you can lift. Now, a puzzle. Three verses later, Paul seems to say the opposite: "For every man shall bear his own burden." Which is it? The answer is in the Greek. In verse two, the word for burdens means heavy weights, crushing loads nobody should carry alone. In verse five it's a different word, a load or a pack, which some readers picture as the kit a soldier carries on a march: your own daily load. Paul means both. Carry your own pack: do your own work, own your own choices. And when someone is crushed by a weight too heavy for one person, a grief, an illness, a debt, a failure, get under it with them. The verse just before says who does the lifting: if someone is caught in a fault, restore them gently, remembering you could be next. Bear one another's burdens doesn't mean fix other people. You don't take the weight away. You stand under it with them. Christians have lived this in casseroles after funerals, rides to chemotherapy, rent paid quietly, friends who sit with you on the worst night and say almost nothing. The law of Christ looks a lot like showing up with your end of the couch.
screen: `THE LAW OF CHRIST: CARRY EACH OTHER.` · `TWO WORDS FOR BURDEN.` · `A CRUSHING WEIGHT, AND A DAILY PACK.` · `STAND UNDER IT WITH THEM.` · then, large: `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.`

segments.voice: First, notice your own pack, what's simply yours to carry today, and just name it. Then picture someone you know under a heavy weight right now, illness, grief, money, a child in trouble, a job that's crushing them, and without trying to fix it, ask: where is one corner of this I could lift, a meal, a ride, an hour of childcare, a text that says I'm here? If you pray, hold them before God.
Burden, the word Paul also uses for your own daily load, carried alongside the crushing weights we bear for each other.
Your line: carry each other. Your own pack, and a corner of theirs. See you on day one hundred forty-three.

143.title: When church hurts
143.hook: done with church, not with Christ: the Bible names harm done by religious people, and a bruised reed is not broken
143.carry: a bruised reed he will not break
143.howItsDone: Christians who've been hurt by a church often talk it through with a trusted friend, pastor or counselor outside that congregation; many later find a different church, and many churches now have safeguarding policies and outside reporting for abuse.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two words for burden, and your line: carry each other. Today, a load some people carry out of church, not into it.

The message arrives on a Tuesday. We've decided it's best if you step back from the worship team for now. No call. No conversation. Or it's a sermon that seemed aimed straight at you, in front of everyone. Or a small group that stopped inviting you after the divorce. Or something much worse, that still doesn't get said out loud. There's a short name for this. And there's a line some people say on the way out the door: I'm done with church, not with Jesus. Today, what happens when together goes wrong.
screen: `A MESSAGE ON A TUESDAY.` → `DONE WITH CHURCH, NOT WITH JESUS.` → `WHEN TOGETHER GOES WRONG.`

segments.voice: Church hurt. It's a modern phrase for harm done by a church or by people in it: judgment, gossip, being pushed out, being used, or abuse. The Bible doesn't pretend this can't happen. A psalm says, in the King James Bible: "For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it." It was a friend, someone the writer worshiped beside: "We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company." The prophets aimed some of their sharpest words at religious leaders. Ezekiel cries: "Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves!" And when Matthew describes Jesus, he borrows a line from Isaiah: "A bruised reed shall he not break." A bruised reed is a stem already bent. He doesn't snap it. Many Christians draw a line here that hurt people find freeing: the congregation that failed you is not the whole church, and it isn't Christ. What comes next differs from person to person. Most churches teach that faith is meant to be lived with others, and many people who step away find a different, healthier church in time. Some need a long rest first. Being believed matters more than being argued with. If what happened was abuse, it was not your fault, and telling someone safe outside that church matters. And if the hurt has left you somewhere dark, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `IT WAS NOT AN ENEMY.` · `SHEPHERDS WHO FEED THEMSELVES.` · `A BRUISED REED SHALL HE NOT BREAK.` · `THE CONGREGATION ISN'T CHRIST.`

segments.voice: If a church, or someone in one, once hurt you, let it come to mind only as far as feels safe; you don't have to relive it. Just name it, the way the psalm does, and picture setting it down beside you. If church has only been kind to you, think of someone it wasn't kind to, and hold them gently. If you pray, you can tell God plainly what happened; if you don't, just let yourself be believed, here.
Church hurt. Harm done by a church or by people in it: real, named in the Psalms, and not the same thing as Christ.
Your line: a bruised reed he will not break. Bent is not the same as broken. Day one hundred forty-three.

144.title: The quiet time
144.hook: many Christians keep a morning quiet time: a Bible, a notebook, a coffee
144.howItsDone: Many Christians keep a daily quiet time, often in the morning, reading a short Bible passage, writing in a journal and praying; others pray morning prayer from the daily office or say set morning prayers before icons at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: church hurt, and a stem bent but not snapped. Your line was a bruised reed he will not break. Now the week turns from together to alone.
screen: `A BRUISED REED HE WILL NOT BREAK.`

segments.voice: Six-fifteen in the morning. The house is still dark. A kettle clicks off. Someone sits at the kitchen table with a mug and three things: a Bible with a cracked spine, a cheap notebook, a pen. No phone. Not yet. They read a few verses, sit, write a line or two. Maybe a name they're worried about. Maybe a question. Twenty minutes, sometimes ten, sometimes five. Then the day comes crashing in: kids, email, traffic. Christians in many places start their mornings something like this. In evangelical churches, it has a name: the quiet time.
screen: `SIX-FIFTEEN, STILL DARK.` → `A BIBLE, A NOTEBOOK, A MUG.` → `THEN THE DAY COMES IN.`

segments.voice: The phrase is fairly recent, at home in evangelical churches and student groups. The habit is ancient. The Psalms are full of mornings. Psalm five, in the King James Bible: "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up." The Hebrew word for direct can mean to lay something out in order, like wood arranged for a fire, or a table set for a meal. The psalmist sets out the morning's prayer, then watches for an answer. And Lamentations, a book of grief over a fallen city, still says of God's mercies: "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." That's the logic of first thing. You haven't failed at anything yet. The day hasn't told you who you are. What happens varies, and that's fine. Some read a short passage, often following a plan. Some write in a journal: what the verse said, what's on their mind, a prayer list. Catholics and Anglicans may pray morning prayer from the daily office, with psalms set for each day. Orthodox Christians may stand before icons at home and say the morning prayers. Some just sit in silence with coffee. The common thread isn't the method. It's the order: before the world gets its say, a little quiet gets the first word. Nobody promises it will feel profound. Plenty of mornings are sleepy and blank. People keep it anyway, the way you keep a friendship: by showing up.
screen: `A MODERN NAME, AN ANCIENT HABIT.` · `IN THE MORNING WILL I DIRECT MY PRAYER.` · `READ, WRITE, SIT, OR PRAY THE OFFICE.` · `BEFORE THE WORLD GETS ITS SAY.` · then, large: `NEW EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Open a notebook, a scrap of paper, or your phone's notes with everything else turned off, and write today's date and one honest line: what's on your mind right now. Sit with it without fixing or polishing it, and add one more line if it comes. If you pray, write a name or a need and offer it; if not, let the page hold what you're carrying.
Morning prayer, the daily office some Christians pray at the day's first light: one way among many of giving the morning its first word.
Your line: first thing, a little quiet. New every morning. See you tomorrow.

145.title: Be still (Psalm 46:10)
145.hook: be still, and know that I am God
145.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 46 in times of fear or crisis, and some use 'be still, and know that I am God' as a short prayer in silent or contemplative prayer, repeated slowly with the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quiet time, with morning prayer among its forms. Your line was first thing, a little quiet.

You've probably seen these words on a mug, a throw pillow, a calm lake photo, in soft script: be still, and know that I am God. It looks like a spa brochure. Here's the surprise. The psalm that line comes from doesn't picture a quiet lake. It pictures the ground giving way, and a war. Mountains sliding into the sea. Nations raging. Kingdoms toppling. Bows, spears and chariots. And in the middle of all that noise, God speaks two words.
screen: `ON A MUG, BY A CALM LAKE.` → `BUT THE PSALM IS LOUD.` → `EARTHQUAKE AND WAR.`

segments.voice: Psalm forty-six opens, in the King James Bible: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." Then it gets loud. "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." The waters roar, the nations rage, kingdoms are moved, the earth melts. Then the psalm turns: God "maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder." Only then comes verse ten: "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth." In Hebrew, be still is one word, harpu. Its root means to let go, to sink down, to let your hands drop, like soldiers told to lower their weapons, or someone unclenching after hours gripping the wheel. So it's less relax, more stop. Drop it. Some scholars think it's spoken first to the warring nations: stop fighting, and know who's God. Others hear it spoken to the frightened people inside the city. Plenty of readers hear both. This stillness isn't calm scenery. It's what happens when you stop trying to hold up the mountains yourself. Martin Luther loved this psalm; his great hymn A Mighty Fortress Is Our God grew out of it. Jews and Christians alike have prayed it in wartime, in plague and in grief. The pillow isn't wrong. It's just missing the earthquake, and the stillness is meant for the moment everything is shaking.
screen: `A VERY PRESENT HELP IN TROUBLE.` · `MOUNTAINS INTO THE SEA.` · `HARPU — LET GO, DROP YOUR HANDS.` · `STILLNESS IN THE EARTHQUAKE.` · then, large: `BE STILL, AND KNOW THAT I AM GOD.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open in your lap, and notice where you're gripping, your jaw, your shoulders, your hands; let each one drop, the way the Hebrew word suggests. Think of the thing that's shaking in your life right now, and don't solve it; just stop holding it up for a while. If you pray, say the line slowly, once, be still, and know that I am God, and then stay still; if you don't pray, just stay.
Be still. In Hebrew, harpu: let go, drop your hands. Said in the middle of an earthquake and a war.
Your line: be still, and know. The mountains were never yours to hold up. That's day one hundred forty-five.

146.title: Why fast (Matthew 6:16–18)
146.hook: Jesus says when you fast, not if: quietly, without a gloomy face
146.howItsDone: Many Christians fast by skipping meals or certain foods on set days or seasons, spending the time in prayer, and many give up a comfort instead when fasting from food isn't safe for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: harpu, let go and drop your hands, said in the middle of an earthquake. Your line was be still, and know.

Skipping lunch is easy to announce. "Oh, I'm not eating today." A little sigh. A small pause, in case anyone asks why. Some people do their diet or their detox out loud. Now go to Jesus on a hillside in Galilee, teaching a crowd. He gets to fasting and doesn't explain it. He assumes it. Not if you fast. When. Then he goes straight for the performance: people who look hungry on purpose, faces smudged and gloomy, so everyone can tell how holy they are. Do the opposite, he says.
screen: `I'M NOT EATING TODAY. SIGH.` → `NOT IF YOU FAST. WHEN.` → `THE GLOOMY FACE.`

segments.voice: Fasting means going without food, or some food, for a time, for the sake of prayer. In Matthew six, in the King James Bible: "Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast." Then: "But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret." Look normal: the same pattern as giving in secret a few lines earlier. Of those who fast for show, Jesus says: "They have their reward." Jesus himself fasted: before his ministry began, the gospels say he spent forty days in the wilderness and was hungry afterward. Moses fasted on the mountain. Elijah walked forty days on the strength of one meal. Esther asked her people to fast before she risked her life. Jesus stands inside that tradition. Why choose hunger? Christians give a few reasons. Hunger clears the head; it reminds you that you're a body, dependent, not in control. Every pang becomes a small bell calling you back to prayer: hunger can pray. Fasting also makes room: the time and money you'd spend on food can go to someone else. And it's a way of saying, with your whole body, that you mean it. A caution many churches give: fasting is not a diet, and it's not for everyone. People who are pregnant, ill or recovering from an eating disorder are usually told not to fast from food at all. Many choose to fast from something else instead.
screen: `GOING WITHOUT, FOR PRAYER.` · `WASH THY FACE. LOOK NORMAL.` · `MOSES, ELIJAH, ESTHER, JESUS.` · `EVERY PANG A SMALL BELL.` · then, large: `WHEN YE FAST.`

segments.voice: Think of one small comfort you reach for without thinking, the second coffee, the snack at three, the scroll before bed, and pick one. Picture the moment later today when you reach for it and find a small ache instead. If you pray, let that ache become a short prayer; if you don't, let it be a moment of noticing.

147.title: Fasting across the church
147.hook: Orthodox Christians fast most Wednesdays and Fridays; Catholics fast in Lent; many Protestants fast for a cause
147.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians fast from meat and dairy on most Wednesdays and Fridays and during several seasons; Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and avoid meat on Lenten Fridays; many Protestants keep Lent or fast together for a particular need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jesus saying when you fast, not if, with a washed face. Your line was hunger can pray.

What's for dinner on a fast day? It depends whose kitchen you're in. A Greek grandmother is cooking beans and greens in water, no meat, no cheese, no olive oil even, as she has on Wednesdays and Fridays for most of her life. A Catholic family is having fish sticks, because it's a Friday in Lent. A young couple from a Baptist church have skipped lunch all week, joining their congregation in praying for a friend with cancer. Very different menus. All of them would call it fasting.
screen: `A GREEK KITCHEN: BEANS, NO OIL.` → `A CATHOLIC KITCHEN: FISH IN LENT.` → `A BAPTIST COUPLE: NO LUNCH ALL WEEK.`

segments.voice: Start early. An ancient Christian handbook called the Didache tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays. Tradition links Friday with the day Jesus died, and Wednesday with the day he was betrayed. That weekly rhythm is still alive. Orthodox churches keep a long fasting calendar: on most Wednesdays and Fridays of the year, through Great Lent before Easter and in several other seasons, Orthodox Christians set aside meat and dairy, and often fish, wine and olive oil. It's done in community, and people are told to adjust for health and circumstance. Catholic rules today center on a few days. On Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, adults fast: one full meal and two small ones. On Fridays in Lent, no meat, which is why parish fish fries turn up in Lent. Giving up something personal for Lent is a familiar Catholic custom too. Protestant churches vary widely. Anglicans, Lutherans and Methodists often keep Lent; the early Methodists fasted on Fridays, and John Wesley urged it. Some evangelical and Pentecostal churches call a fast for a specific need: a sick friend, a decision, a new year. Some follow the pattern of Daniel, who said: "I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth." The rules differ. Underneath, each tradition is clearing something away, food, time, a habit, to make space: for prayer, for hunger to remind you, and for others.
screen: `THE DIDACHE: WEDNESDAYS AND FRIDAYS.` · `ORTHODOX: A LONG FASTING CALENDAR.` · `CATHOLICS: FRIDAYS IN LENT.` · `PROTESTANTS: FASTING FOR A CAUSE.` · then, large: `MAKE SPACE.`

segments.voice: Picture this month's calendar and pick one day on it, maybe a Wednesday or a Friday, the Didache's days. Ask what you could fast from that day, meat, sugar, coffee, your phone after dinner, streaming, shopping, and choose one, noticing how it feels to decide in advance. If you pray, offer that day to God now; if you don't, simply mark it as a day to make space.
Didache, an ancient Christian handbook that told believers to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, the start of a rhythm kept in many forms since.
Your line: make space. A calendar of fasts or none, the idea underneath is the same. Until tomorrow.
